turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Ag, sorry we're late, doc. The robot by the Spar was out, and then the parking machine wouldn't take my card, so my wife had to dash back to the bakkie for coins.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): No stress at all, Mr Dlamini. Come sit. How's the traffic been treating you otherwise?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Shame, it's been hectic this whole week with the school holidays. The N2 was bumper to bumper even at half past nine, and we just sat there.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ja, I know that feeling. So, what brings you in today?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Well, it's the hand, really. The left one. It's still a bit weak, three months after that mild stroke, and I keep dropping things.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me a bit more about the weakness.

[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): It's not terrible, hey. I can still hold a cup of coffee, but buttons are a mission, and when I try to... um, when I try to open a jar my wife has to finish it. It started, well the stroke was in March, so about three months, and the hand never quite came right like the leg did.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the walking?

[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Walking is okay. I go to the shops most mornings, a bit slower than before, no stick, and I haven't fallen. My wife walks with me on the weekends down by the promenade, which is nice except when the wind...
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm.
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): ...comes off the sea and it's freezing. But ja, the legs feel steady enough for that.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): How about your speech? Any slurring, or words getting stuck?

[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Speech is fine now. For about ten days after the stroke I was slurring a bit, my brother said I sounded drunk, which was embarrassing at the braai, but that cleared. I don't slur anymore.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any headaches?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no headaches.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest pain, or shortness of breath when you walk?

[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No chest pain. And I'm not short of breath, even up the stairs at home. We live in a double storey in Plumstead, so the stairs are there every day, and I manage them fine.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the medicines, what are you actually taking?

[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Aspirin, a hundred milligrams, one in the morning with breakfast, the little cardio one from the chemist. Then atorvastin, sorry atorvastatin, forty milligrams at night for the cholesterol. And the blood pressure tablet, amlodopine, five milligrams, also in the morning.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Amlodipine five milligrams every morning, and the statin at night. Any misses?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't think I miss them. My wife sets them out in one of those weekly boxes, Monday to Sunday, so if I forget she...
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): ...she notices before I leave for my walk. So pretty much every day.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you had any other operations, or is the stroke the main thing in the history?

[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Appendix out when I was twenty two, that's the only operation. And the high blood pressure has been there for, ag, years and years, they picked it up at a work medical before I retired from the railways.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Family side, anyone with strokes or heart trouble?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): My older brother, Piet, he had a heart attack at fifty eight. He's fine now, lives in George. My dad died of old age, nothing like this.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or drink much?

[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): I stopped smoking in two thousand and ten, used to be about ten a day. Now I have a glass of red wine with supper, maybe four nights a week, not more. My wife is stricter than the doctor was, hey.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me just take your blood pressure while we talk. Arm out for me.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): This arm? The right one is easier, the left still feels funny when you squeeze it.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ja, right arm is perfect. Sit quiet a second.
[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): I was saying to my wife in the waiting room, the magazines are all from last year, and the sister at reception was so kind, she...
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, that's one thirty six over eighty two. Pulse is seventy four.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Is that alright? Last time at the clinic it was higher, like one fifty something, but that was when I was stressed after the hospital.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Today's reading is fine for where we are. Let me check the hand. Squeeze my fingers.
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Like this? I can do it but it feels softer on the left.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ja, left grip is a little weaker than the right. No droop of the face, and your speech sounds clear to me sitting here.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): That's a relief, because I keep worrying it's starting again, especially when I drop the teaspoon in the morning.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): I think this is leftover weakness from that mild stroke, not a new one. The fact the leg and the speech came back, and it's only the hand lingering, fits with that.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): So I don't need to panic every time I fumble a button.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): No. Keep doing the hand exercises the physio showed you, little and often, and keep walking like you are.

[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): She said squeeze a soft ball, twenty times, three times a day. I've been a bit slack on the evenings if I'm watching the rugby, I'll be honest, the Stormers game just runs on.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Try not to skip those. I'll book a cholesterol blood test, the lipids, so we can see if the 40 milligrams is enough.
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): At the lab downstairs, or do I go to PathCare?
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Reception will book it with PathCare, this week if they can. And we might do a scan of the head if the hand does not settle by the time I see you again.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): A scan. Like the one in the hospital? That machine was so loud I nearly...
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Only if it hasn't improved. I'm not ordering it today. Come back and see me in six weeks, we'll look at the hand and the bloods together.
[SEG0049] person_1 (PATIENT): Six weeks. Should I bring my wife in next time? She remembers the dates better than I do, and she wanted to ask about...
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): She's welcome. If the weakness suddenly gets worse, or the speech goes funny again, or you can't walk properly, don't wait for that appointment, go to casualty.
[SEG0051] person_1 (PATIENT): Casualty at Groote Schuur, ja. I'll tell her. Thanks, doc, I feel a bit less wound up than when I walked in.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. See you in six weeks, Mr Dlamini. Drive safe.

spec.situation: Patient three months after a mild stroke with a spouse; slight weakness in the left hand; takes aspirin, atorvastatin and an amlodipine tablet; blood pressure read aloud; walking and speech discussed.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

bad.reason: Wife and double-storey house in Plumstead supported; living together not explicitly stated.
bad.text: living (description=Lives with his wife in a double-storey house in Plumstead, status=current, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Patient denied current slurring, specifically 'I don't slur anymore.'
